{{short description|Generalized concept of a set element}}
{{for|elements in a set|Element (mathematics)}}{{for|components of the Periodic Table|Chemical element}}

In [[category theory]], the concept of an '''element''', or a '''point''', generalizes the more usual [[set theory|set theoretic]] concept of an [[element (mathematics)|element]] of a [[set (mathematics)|set]] to an [[object (category theory)|object]] of any [[category (mathematics)|category]].  This idea often allows restating of definitions or properties of [[morphism]]s (such as [[monomorphism]] or [[product (category theory)|product]]) given by a [[universal property]] in more familiar terms, by stating their relation to elements.  Some very general theorems, such as [[Yoneda's lemma]] and the [[Mitchell embedding theorem]], are of great utility for this, by allowing one to work in a context where these translations are valid.  This approach to category theory – in particular the use of the Yoneda lemma in this way – is due to [[Grothendieck]], and is often called the method of the '''functor of points'''.

== Definition ==
Suppose '''C''' is any [[category (mathematics)|category]] and ''A'', ''T'' are two objects of '''C'''.  A ''T''-valued point of ''A'' is simply a morphism {{nowrap|''p'' : ''T'' → ''A''}}.  The set of all ''T''-valued points of ''A'' varies [[functor]]ially with ''T'', giving rise to the "functor of points" of ''A''; according to the [[Yoneda lemma]], this completely determines ''A'' as an object of '''C'''.

== Properties of morphisms ==
Many properties of morphisms can be restated in terms of points.  For example, a map ''f'' is said to be a [[monomorphism]] if
: For all maps ''g'', ''h'', if {{nowrap|1=''f'' ∘ ''g'' = ''f'' ∘ ''h''}} then {{nowrap|1=''g'' = ''h''}}.
Suppose {{nowrap|''f'' : ''B'' → ''C''}} and {{nowrap|''g'', ''h'' : ''A'' → ''B''}} in ''C''.  Then ''g'' and ''h'' are ''A''-valued points of ''B'', and therefore monomorphism is equivalent to the more familiar statement
: ''f'' is a monomorphism if it is an [[injective function]] on points of ''B''.
Some care is necessary.  ''f'' is an [[epimorphism]] if the [[dual (category theory)|dual]] condition holds:
: For all maps ''g'', ''h'' (of some suitable type), {{nowrap|1=''g'' ∘ ''f'' = ''h'' ∘ ''f''}} implies {{nowrap|1=''g'' = ''h''}}.
In set theory, the term "epimorphism" is synonymous with "[[surjection]]", i.e.
: Every point of ''C'' is the [[image (mathematics)|image]], under ''f'', of some point of ''B''.
This is clearly not the translation of the first statement into the language of points, and in fact these statements are ''not'' equivalent in general.  However, in some contexts, such as [[abelian categories]], "monomorphism" and "epimorphism" are backed by sufficiently strong conditions that in fact they do allow such a reinterpretation on points.

Similarly, [[category theory|categorical]] constructions such as the [[product (category theory)|product]] have pointed analogues.  Recall that if ''A'', ''B'' are two objects of '''C''', their product {{nowrap|''A'' × ''B''}} is an object such that
: There exist maps {{nowrap|''p'' : ''A'' × ''B'' → ''A''}}, {{nowrap|''q'' : ''A'' × ''B'' → ''B''}}, and for any ''T'' and maps {{nowrap|''f'' : ''T'' → ''A''}}, {{nowrap|''g'' : ''T'' → ''B''}}, there exists a unique map {{nowrap|''h'' : ''T'' → ''A'' × ''B''}} such that {{nowrap|1=''f'' = ''p'' ∘ ''h''}} and {{nowrap|1=''g'' = ''q'' ∘ ''h''}}.
In this definition, ''f'' and ''g'' are ''T''-valued points of ''A'' and ''B'', respectively, while ''h'' is a ''T''-valued point of ''A'' × ''B''.  An alternative definition of the product is therefore:
: ''A'' × ''B'' is an object of '''C''', together with projection maps {{nowrap|''p'' : ''A'' × ''B'' → ''A''}} and {{nowrap|''q'' : ''A'' × ''B'' → ''B''}}, such that ''p'' and ''q'' furnish a [[bijection]] between points of {{nowrap|''A'' × ''B''}} and ''pairs of points'' of ''A'' and ''B''.
This is the more familiar definition of the [[Cartesian product|product]] of two sets.

== Geometric origin ==
{{see also|Rational point}}
The terminology is geometric in origin; in [[algebraic geometry]], Grothendieck introduced the notion of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] in order to unify the subject with [[arithmetic geometry]], which dealt with the same idea of studying solutions to [[polynomial equation]]s (i.e. [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]]) but where the solutions are not [[complex number]]s but [[rational number]]s, [[integer]]s, or even elements of some [[finite field]].  A scheme is then just that: a scheme for collecting together all the manifestations of a variety defined by the same equations but with solutions taken in different number sets.  One scheme gives a complex variety, whose points are its {{nowrap|(Spec '''C''')}}-valued points, as well as the set of {{nowrap|(Spec '''Q''')}}-valued points (rational solutions to the equations), and even {{nowrap|(Spec '''F'''<sub>''p''</sub>)}}-valued points (solutions [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] ''p'').

One feature of the language of points is evident from this example: it is, in general, not enough to consider just points with values in a single object.  For example, the equation {{nowrap|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> + 1 = 0}} (which defines a scheme) has no [[real number|real]] solutions, but it has complex solutions, namely ±''i''.  It also has one solution modulo 2 and two modulo 5, 13, 29, etc. (all [[prime number|primes]] that are 1 modulo 4).  Just taking the real solutions would give no information whatsoever.

== Relation with set theory ==
The situation is analogous to the case where '''C''' is the category '''Set''', [[category of sets|of sets]] of actual elements.  In this case, we have the "one-pointed" set {{mset|1}}, and the elements of any set ''S'' are the same as the {{nowrap|{{mset|1}}-valued}} points of ''S''.  In addition, though, there are the {{nowrap|{{mset|1, 2}}-valued}} points, which are pairs of elements of ''S'', or elements of {{nowrap|''S'' × ''S''}}.  In the context of sets, these higher points are extraneous: ''S'' is determined completely by its {{nowrap|{1}-points}}.  However, as shown above, this is special (in this case, it is because all sets are iterated [[coproduct]]s of {{mset|1}}).
